chunks: We said: Fear from their enemies did not threaten his holy forefathers (a.s),
as they adhered to dissimulation (taqiyyah) and ostensibly retracted from the claim of Imamate and exiled it from themselves,
whereas, the Imam of the Age faces every fear, because he is the one to rise with the sword and raise the call for his leadership and fight his adversaries.
Where is the similarity between his fear from his enemies and the fear of his forefathers, if there is no scarcity of reflection?
Moreover, when anyone of his forefathers (a.s) was murdered or died, there was someone qualified for Imamate from their progeny to replace him and fill his position,
whereas the case of the Master of the Age is diametrically opposite to this,
since it is well-known that no one is to succeed him and take his position.
Therefore, the difference between the two instances is clear.

key_terms.الإِمَامَة: Imamate, the divinely appointed leadership and authority
key_terms.التَّقِيَّة: Dissimulation or concealment of faith/status to avoid harm
key_terms.صَاحِبُ الأَمْرِ: The Master of the Age, referring to Imam al-Mahdi (a.s)
key_terms.يَسُدُّ مَسَدَّهُ: To fill his position or succeed him

ai.seo_question: Why is the fear of the Imam of the Age greater than that of his forefathers?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi highlights the unique eschatological burden of Imam al-Zaman (a.s.), whose fear stems not from dissimulation but from the finality of his leadership and the absence of a successor to assume the Imamate. Unlike previous Imams who could conceal their status or be succeeded, the Mahdi’s public manifestation through the sword and his solitary role intensify the existential weight of his leadership. This distinction underscores the theological necessity of the Occultation as a period of divine protection before the final, irreversible appearance.
